en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 5: The Discourse on Being Without Blemish (Anaṅgaṇasutta) Thus have I heard: [a certain time] the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is without blemish, he dwells with a mind that is well-released in two ways. What two? He dwells with a mind well-released through the destruction of craving, and he dwells with a mind well-released through the destruction of the underlying tendencies. When a bhikkhu is without blemish, he dwells with a mind well-released in these two ways. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu without blemish? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned the five lower fetters, and he is one who will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is without blemish. When a bhikkhu is without blemish, he dwells with a mind well-released in two ways. What two? He dwells with a mind well-released through the destruction of craving, and he dwells with a mind well-released through the destruction of the underlying tendencies. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu dwell with a mind well-released through the destruction of craving? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned craving for sensual pleasures; he has cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. He has abandoned craving for existence; he has cut it off at the root... done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. He has abandoned craving for non-existence; he has cut it off at the root... done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-released through the destruction of craving. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu dwell with a mind well-released through the destruction of the underlying tendencies? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasures; he has cut it off at the root... done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. He has abandoned the underlying tendency to aversion toward forms; he has cut it off at the root... done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. He has abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit regarding form; he has cut it off at the root... done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. He has abandoned the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding form; he has cut it off at the root... done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-released through the destruction of the underlying tendencies. When a bhikkhu is without blemish, he dwells with a mind well-released in these two ways. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus!”
“Friends,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, these four types of persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four?
Here, friends, a certain person who is actually possessed of a blemish does not understand, as it really is, that "there is a blemish within me.
But here, friends, a certain person who is actually possessed of a blemish understands, as it really is, that "there is a blemish within me."
"Here, friends, a certain person who is actually blemished does not understand, as it really is, that 'there is no blemish within me.
But here, friends, another person who is actually free from blemish understands, as it really is, that 'there is no blemish within me.

Now, friends, of these two persons, the one who is actually blemished and yet does not understand, as it really is, that 'there is a blemish within me,' is declared to be the inferior person between these two who are both blemished."

In this regard, friends, that person who, while still having a blemish, understands as it truly is: "There is a blemish within me"—this one, among these two persons who both have blemishes, is declared the superior person.

In this regard, friends, that person who, being without a blemish, does not understand as it truly is: "There is no blemish within me"—this one, among these two persons who both are without blemishes, is declared the inferior person.

"In this regard, friend, that person who, being free from blemish, understands as it really is: 'There is no blemish within me'—this one, among these two persons who are both free from blemish, is declared the superior person.
When this was said, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to the Venerable Sāriputta:

"What, friend Sāriputta, is the cause, what is the reason, why between these two persons who are both possessed of a blemish, one is declared the inferior person and the other is declared the superior person?"
“But what, friend Sāriputta, is the cause, what is the reason why, of these two persons who are both without blemish, one is declared a base person and the other is declared a superior person?
“In this case, friend, regarding that person who, while actually having a blemish within, does not understand as it really is:
‘There is a blemish within me’—it is to be expected that he will not generate desire [to remove it], will not exert effort, and will not arouse energy.”
He will not strive for the abandoning of that blemish;
he will pass away with a mind possessed of lust, possessed of hatred, possessed of delusion, possessed of blemish, and defiled.
It is just as if, friends, a bronze bowl were brought from a marketplace or a smith’s workshop, covered all over with dust and dirt.
"If its owners neither used it nor polished it, and they were to place it on a dusty road,
would that bronze bowl, friend, become even more defiled and covered in grime after some time?
"It would, friend."
“In the same way, friend, when a person who has a blemish does not understand as it really is:
‘I have a blemish within,’ it can be expected that he will not generate desire, will not exert effort,
and will not arouse energy for the sake of abandoning that blemish.
Such a person will die with lust, with hatred, with delusion, with blemish, and with a defiled mind.
In this regard, friends, for that person who, while still possessing a blemish, understands as it really is:
"There is a blemish within me"—it is to be expected that he will generate desire, exert effort, and arouse energy.
For the sake of abandoning that blemish,
he will pass away with a mind free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, free from blemish, and undefiled— just as if, friends,
a bronze bowl were brought from a marketplace or a smith’s workshop, covered over with dust and grime.
“If their owners were to use it and polish it, and did not set it down on a dusty road,
would that bronze bowl, friend, become even more pure and bright after some time?”—
“Yes, friend.”
“In the same way, friends, when a person who has an internal blemish understands as it really is:
‘I have an internal blemish,’ it is to be expected that he will generate desire, exert effort,
and arouse energy for the sake of abandoning that blemish.”
Thus, being without lust, without hatred, without delusion, without blemish, and with a mind undefiled, he will pass away.
In this regard, friends, it is to be expected that a person who, though being without blemish, does not understand as it really is:
"There is no blemish within me," will attend to a sign of beauty; and because of that sign of beauty...
If, through such mental attention, lust should arise in his mind,
he will pass away with a mind possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion, accompanied by blemish and defilement.
It is just as if, friends, a bronze bowl were brought from a marketplace or a smith’s workshop, pure and bright.
"If its owners neither used it nor polished it, and they were to place it in a dusty place,
would that bronze bowl, friend, become even more defiled and covered with grime after some time?
"It would, friend."

“In the same way, friend, when a person who is actually free from blemish does not understand as it really is: ‘There is no blemish within me,’ it is to be expected that he will attend to a sign of beauty;
through attending to that sign of beauty, lust will surge up in his mind.
He will die with lust, with hatred, with delusion, with blemish, and with a defiled mind.
In this regard, friends, for that person who is actually without blemish and understands as it truly is:
"There is no blemish within me"—it is to be expected that he will not attend to the sign of the beautiful; and because of that non-attention to the sign of the beautiful...
Through non-attention, lust will not agitate the mind;
he will pass away free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, free from defilement, with a mind that is undefiled.
Just as, friends, a bronze bowl might be brought from a shop or a smith’s workshop, pure and bright.
“If their owners were to use it and polish it, and did not set it down on the dusty road,
would that bronze bowl, friend, become even more pure and bright at a later time?”—
“Yes, friend.”

“In the same way, friend, when a person who is actually free from blemish understands as it really is: ‘There is no blemish within me,’ it can be expected of him that he will not attend to the sign of the beautiful;
because of his non-attention to the sign of the beautiful, lust will not agitate his mind.
Thus, being free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, without blemish, and with a mind undefiled, he will pass away.
This, friend Moggallāna, is the cause, this is the reason why, of these two persons who both possess blemishes, one is declared a base person and the other is declared a superior person.
But this, friend Moggallāna, is the cause, this is the reason why, of these two persons who both are without blemish, one is declared a base person and the other is declared a superior person.”
“‘Stain, stain,’ friend, it is said.
Of what now, friend, is this the designation: namely, ‘stain’?
“This, friend, is the designation for evil, unwholesome states that fall within the sphere of desire; namely, ‘stain.’”
“Furthermore, friends, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise as this:
‘O, may I commit an offense, yet may the bhikkhus not know that I have committed an offense.
And it is also possible, friends, that the bhikkhus would come to know of that bhikkhu.”
‘I have fallen into an offense.
Thinking, ‘The monks know that I have fallen into an offense,’ he becomes angry and displeased.
"Friend, both anger and resentment—these two are stains.
However, friend, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise: [that he might not have these stains]."
‘May it be that I have committed an offense, so that the monks might admonish me in private, not in the midst of the Saṅgha.
Yet, friends, it is possible that the monks might admonish that monk in the midst of the Saṅgha, not in private. [Thinking:
‘The monks are admonishing me in the midst of the Saṅgha, not in private’—”
Thus he becomes angry and displeased.
Now, friends, both anger and resentment—
both of these are stains.
"It is indeed possible, friends, that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise:
'Oh, may I commit an offense, but may one who has a counterpart charge me, not one who lacks a counterpart.
It is also indeed possible, friends, that a bhikkhu who lacks a counterpart might charge him, and not one who has a counterpart."
‘A person who is without equal reproaches me, not one who has an equal’—
thus he becomes angry and displeased.
Now, friends, that which is anger and that which is resentment—
Both of these are flaws.
However, friends, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might have this wish arise:
"Oh, that the Teacher would teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus by repeatedly questioning me alone, and not by repeatedly questioning some other bhikkhu!"

"It is indeed possible, friends, that the Teacher might question one monk repeatedly and teach the Dhamma to the monks, yet he does not question this particular monk repeatedly and teach the Dhamma to the monks. [One might think:
'The Teacher questions another monk repeatedly and teaches the Dhamma to the monks, but he does not question me repeatedly and teach the Dhamma to the monks.'"
Thus he becomes angry and displeased.
Now, friends, both anger and resentment—
both of these are stains.
"It is possible, friends, that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise:
‘Oh, may the bhikkhus enter the village for alms-food placing me alone at their head, and not some other bhikkhu!
And it is also possible, friends, that the bhikkhus might enter the village for alms-food placing some other bhikkhu at their head."
They might enter a village for almsfood; they would not enter that village for almsfood with other monks preceding them and preceding them. [Thinking:
"The monks enter the village for almsfood with another monk preceding them and preceding them; they do not enter the village for almsfood with me preceding them and preceding them."
Thus he becomes angry and displeased.
Now, friends, both anger and resentment—
both of these are stains.
"It is possible, friends, that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise as this:
‘Oh, may I alone receive the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood in the meal hall, and may no other bhikkhu receive the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood in the meal hall.

And it is also possible, friends, that another bhikkhu might receive the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood in the meal hall, while that bhikkhu does not receive the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood in the meal hall."
‘Another monk receives the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food in the dining hall, but I do not receive the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food in the dining hall’—
thus he becomes angry and dissatisfied. Now, friends, that which is anger and that which is resentment—
Both of these are flaws.
Furthermore, friends, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise:
"Oh, that I alone, having eaten in the meal hall, should give the blessing; may no other bhikkhu, having eaten in the meal hall, give the blessing."

But it is possible, friends, that another bhikkhu might offer the expression of appreciation after eating in the meal hall, while this bhikkhu does not offer the expression of appreciation after eating in the meal hall.

Thinking, "Another bhikkhu offers the expression of appreciation after eating in the meal hall, but I do not offer the expression of appreciation after eating in the meal hall," he becomes angry and displeased.
"Friend, both anger and resentment—these two are stains.
Moreover, friend, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise: [that others would not think ill of him, etc.]"
‘Oh, that I alone might teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have come to the monastery, and that no other bhikkhu should teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have come to the monastery!

Yet it is possible, friends, that another bhikkhu might teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have come to the monastery, and that this bhikkhu would not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have come to the monastery. [Thinking:
‘Another bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have come to the monastery; I do not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have come to the monastery.’”
Thus he becomes angry and displeased.
Now, friends, both anger and resentment—
both of these are stains.
"Furthermore, friends, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise as this:
'O, that I alone might teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhunīs who have come to the monastery...
[and so on] ...teach the Dhamma to the laymen...'"
‘I shall teach the Dhamma to the female lay followers; no other bhikkhu shall teach the Dhamma to the female lay followers who have come to the monastery.

Yet it is possible, friend, that another bhikkhu might teach the Dhamma to the female lay followers who have come to the monastery, while that bhikkhu does not teach the Dhamma to the female lay followers who have come to the monastery. [Thinking:
‘Another bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the female lay followers who have come to the monastery; I do not teach the Dhamma to the female lay followers who have come to the monastery.’”
Thus he becomes angry and displeased.
Now, friends, both anger and resentment—
both of these are stains.
"Furthermore, friends, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise as this:
‘Oh, may the bhikkhus honor, respect, revere, and venerate me alone; may they not honor, respect, revere, and venerate another bhikkhu.’"
"It is indeed possible, friends, that other monks might honor, respect, revere, and venerate another monk, while they do not honor, respect, revere, and venerate this monk.
Thinking, 'The monks honor, respect, revere, and venerate another monk, but they do not honor, respect, revere,
and venerate me,' he becomes angry and displeased."
"Friends, both anger and resentment—these two are stains.
Yet it is possible, friends, that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise: [that he would not have these stains]."
‘Oh, that the bhikkhunīs … the male lay followers … the female lay followers would honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me alone, and would not honor, respect, esteem, and venerate another bhikkhu!’”
"Furthermore, friends, it is possible that lay followers might honor, respect, revere, and venerate another monk, yet they do not honor, respect, revere, and venerate this monk. Thinking,
'The lay followers honor, respect, revere, and venerate another monk, but they do not honor, respect, revere,
and venerate me,' he becomes angry and displeased."
"Friends, both anger and resentment—both these are stains.
Yet, friends, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise: [that 'I would not be angry or resentful toward anyone at all']."
‘Oh, may I alone be the recipient of excellent robes, and may no other bhikkhu be the recipient of excellent robes!
Yet it is possible, friends, that another bhikkhu might be the recipient of excellent robes while this bhikkhu is not the recipient of excellent robes. [To think:
‘Another bhikkhu is the recipient of excellent robes, but I am not the recipient of excellent robes’—”
Thus he becomes angry and displeased.
Now, friends, both anger and resentment—
both of these are stains.
"It is indeed possible, friends, that a certain bhikkhu here might have such a wish arise as this:
‘Oh, may I alone be the recipient of exquisite almsfood... [and so on] ...may I alone be the recipient of exquisite lodgings...’"
‘May another bhikkhu be the recipient of excellent requisites for the sick— medicines and provisions— and may this bhikkhu not be the recipient of excellent requisites for the sick—
medicines and provisions. Yet, friend, it is possible that another bhikkhu might be the recipient of excellent requisites for the sick—
medicines and provisions— while that bhikkhu is not the recipient of excellent requisites for the sick— medicines and provisions.”
‘Another bhikkhu is a recipient of excellent requisites for the sick, including medicines, whereas I am not a recipient of excellent requisites for the sick, including medicines’—
thus he becomes angry and dissatisfied. Now, friends, that which is anger and that which is dissatisfaction—
Both of these are stains.
"Stain," friends, is a designation for these evil, unwholesome spheres of desire.
For any monk, friends, in whom these evil, unwholesome spheres of desire are seen to be unabandoned...
Even though they may speak well, even if he is one who dwells in the forest, stays in remote lodgings, is an alms-collector,
goes on a continuous round for alms, wears rag-robes, and wears coarse robes— nevertheless, his fellow celibates do not honor him,
do not revere him, do not esteem him, and do not worship him.
For what reason?
Because those evil, unwholesome tendencies of longing belonging to that venerable one are seen and heard to be unabandoned.
It is just as if, friends, a bronze bowl were brought from a marketplace or a smith’s workshop, pure and bright.
Suppose its owners were to prepare a snake carcass, a dog carcass, or a human carcass, cover it with another bronze bowl, and enter the marketplace.
Seeing this, people would say:
"Hey, what is being carried here? It looks like something precious!"
Suppose someone were to rise up, open it, and look inside.
At the mere sight of it, a sense of displeasure would arise within him, a sense of repulsion would arise, and a sense of loathing would arise;
even those who are hungry would have no desire to eat, let alone those who are already full.
In the same way, friends, if these evil, unwholesome spheres of desire are seen and heard to be unabandoned in any bhikkhu,
then even if he is a forest-dweller, one who stays in remote lodgings, an alms-collector who goes on a continuous round for alms,
a wearer of rag-robes, or a wearer of coarse robes, his fellow celibates will neither honor nor revere him.
They neither honor, respect, nor worship him.
Why is that? Because those evil, unwholesome tendencies of desire belonging to that venerable one are seen and heard to be unabandoned.
Friends, when these evil, unwholesome spheres of desire are seen and heard to have been abandoned by any bhikkhu whatsoever,
even if he is a village-dweller, one who accepts invitations to meals, and one who wears robes given by householders,
his fellow celibates still honor him, revere him, esteem him, and worship him.
And why is that? Because those evil, unwholesome tendencies of desire belonging to that venerable one are seen and heard to have been abandoned.
It is just as if, friends, a bronze bowl were brought from a marketplace or a smith’s workshop, pure and bright.

Suppose its owners, having prepared boiled rice of the finest quality—free from black grains and served with many soups and many curries—were to place it in another bronze bowl and cover it, then set out into the marketplace.
Seeing this, people would say:
"Hey, what is being carried here? It looks like something very precious!"
Suppose someone were to rise up, open it, and look inside.
At the mere sight of it, a sense of attractiveness would arise, a sense of non-disgust would arise, and a sense of non-repulsion would arise;
even those who are well-fed would have a desire to eat, let alone those who are hungry.
In the same way, friends, if these evil, unwholesome spheres of desire are seen and heard to have been abandoned by any bhikkhu,
then even if he is a village-dweller, one who accepts invitations for meals, and one who wears robes given by householders,
his fellow celibates still honor him, revere him, esteem him, and worship him.
"And for what reason?
Because those evil, unwholesome tendencies of desire belonging to that venerable one are seen to have been abandoned, and they are also heard to have been abandoned.
When this was said, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, an analogy occurs to me.
“Let it occur to you, friend Moggallāna.
“Friend, on one occasion I was staying at Rājagaha, on Mount Vebhāra.”
Then, friends, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I entered Rājagaha for alms.
Now at that time, Samīti the chariot-maker’s son was planing the felloe of a chariot wheel.
Standing nearby was the Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, formerly a chariot-maker’s son.
Then, friends, this reflection arose in the mind of Paṇḍuputta the Ājīvaka, the son of a former cartwright:
“O, if only this Samīti, the son of a cartwright, would plane away this crookedness, this curvature, and this flaw from this rim!
Then this rim would be free of crookedness, free of curvature, and free of flaws; it would be pure, established in its true essence.”
"In whatever way, friends, the Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, the son of a former wheelwright, had a thought in his mind,
in that very way did Samīti, the son of a wheelwright, plane away the crookedness, the curvature,
and the defect from that rim. Then, friends, the Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, the son of a former wheelwright, being delighted, uttered words of delight:"
‘Having understood heart with heart, as it were, he cuts it away. In the same way, friend,
those persons who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faithlessness, seeking a livelihood rather than out of faith—
those who are fraudulent, deceitful, cunning, restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, and loose of speech, [and who are unrestrained] in their sense faculties...

They do not guard the doors of their sense faculties; they lack moderation in eating; they are not devoted to wakefulness; they have no regard for the state of a recluse; they do not have intense reverence for the training;
they are luxurious and lax; they are leaders in falling away; they have abandoned the burden of solitude; they are indolent and of weak energy;
they are muddle-minded, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, and of poor wisdom—stupid and dull-witted.
To them, the Venerable Sāriputta, as it were, fashions heart with heart by means of this Dhamma exposition, having understood their minds.

And those sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith—those who are not fraudulent, not deceitful, not sycophantic, not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not talkative, not loose-tongued;
who are guarded in the doors of their sense faculties, and moderate in eating;
Devoted to wakefulness, looking toward the state of a recluse, possessing intense reverence for the training, neither luxurious nor lax,
having laid aside the burden of worldly decline, taking solitude as their foremost priority, with energy aroused, self-exerted, established in mindfulness,
clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, wise, and not dull-witted— these venerable ones [repeated] this to the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having heard this discourse on the Dhamma, they seem to drink it in and seem to devour it with both speech and mind, thinking:
"How wonderful, friends! This fellow practitioner, having caused us to emerge from the unwholesome, establishes us in the wholesome.
Just as, friends, a woman or a man—young, youthful, fond of ornaments, and having washed their head—[would take] a garland of blue lotuses...
Just as one who, having received a garland of jasmine, a garland of vassika, or a garland of atimuttaka, would receive it with both hands and place it upon the head—
the highest limb— so too, friends, those clansmen who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, being honest...
They are free from deceit, free from guile, not arrogant, not conceited, not fickle, not talkative, and not loose in speech;
they guard the doors of their sense faculties, are moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, intent upon the state of a recluse, possessing intense reverence for the training,
neither luxurious nor lax, having laid aside the burden of backsliding, taking the lead in seclusion, and being energetic.

“Those who are resolute, established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, wise, and not dull-witted—having heard this Dhamma exposition from the Venerable Sāriputta, they seem to drink it and chew it with both speech and mind, thinking:
‘How wonderful, friends! This fellow practitioner, having made us emerge from the unwholesome, establishes us in the wholesome.’”
Thus both these great nāgas rejoiced in each other’s well-spoken words.
The *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta*, the fifth, is finished.
